content: In low-resource settings, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), an independent body, prioritized updating the 2016 recommendation on routine ultrasound scans. A new systematic review was conducted to evaluate the use of routine ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy. This update was part of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) commitment to evidence-informed policies and its living guidelines approach. The Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research (SRH) and the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA) led the process. The guideline focuses specifically on routine antenatal ultrasound scans before 24 weeks of pregnancy and does not include evidence on the use of Doppler ultrasound for fetal surveillance in cases of growth-restricted fetuses. The recommendations aim to inform national and local health policies and clinical protocols. The target audience includes public health policymakers, program managers, non-governmental organizations, professional societies, healthcare workers (such as obstetricians, midwives, and general practitioners), and academic staff involved in training healthcare workers. The recommendations also guide future research and assess current practices. The updated recommendation applies to all pregnant women and adolescent girls receiving antenatal care (ANC) in healthcare facilities or community-based settings, as well as their fetuses and newborns. The guideline question was prioritized during the development of the 2016 WHO ANC guideline and was later updated in 2019 as part of WHO’s living guideline commitment. The outcomes of interest align with those prioritized in the ANC guideline for ultrasound interventions, including maternal and fetal outcomes such as maternal mortality, detection of fetal anomalies, neonatal mortality, and maternal satisfaction. The recommendation is an update of one of the 49 recommendations published in the 2016 WHO ANC guideline. The development process followed WHO’s standardized operating procedures, including identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for implementation and evaluation. The GSG identified this recommendation as a high priority for updating based on new evidence. The Executive Guideline Steering Group is an independent panel of external experts and stakeholders from WHO’s six regions. This group advises WHO on prioritizing questions in maternal and perinatal health for guideline development or updates. The WHO Steering Group, comprising staff from the SRH and MCA departments, managed the updating process, drafted key questions, and supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis. They also organized technical consultations and finalized the guideline document. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) consisted of 13 external experts and stakeholders, ensuring geographic and gender balance and avoiding conflicts of interest. This diverse group included experts in research, guideline development, clinical policy, and ANC interventions, as well as a patient/consumer representative. The GDG reviewed evidence, interpreted findings, and formulated the final recommendation during an online meeting in June 2021. They also approved the final guideline document before submission to WHO’s Guidelines Review Committee. The External Review Group (ERG) was a geographically and gender-balanced group of four members, including technical experts and stakeholders. They peer-reviewed a preliminary version of the guideline to identify errors and provide feedback on clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. The ERG ensured that the values and preferences of affected individuals, including pregnant women, healthcare workers, and policymakers, were considered. However, the ERG did not alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. The systematic review team and guideline methodologists, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, coordinated the systematic review process. Methodologists from the Evidence-based Medicine Consultancy in the UK appraised quantitative evidence using the GRADE methodology. Qualitative evidence was reviewed by experts from the University of Central Lancashire, synthesizing data on women’s and healthcare workers’ views on ANC. External partners and observers, including representatives from organizations like FIGO, ICM, UNFPA, USAID, ISUOG, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, participated as observers in the final GDG meeting. These organizations are potential implementers of the guideline and have a history of collaboration with WHO. Observers did not participate in formulating recommendations. WHO requires experts in advisory roles to disclose any potential conflicts of interest. All GDG and ERG members, as well as observers, completed and signed declarations of interest (DOI) forms. The WHO Steering Group reviewed these forms to assess the severity of any conflicts and managed them according to WHO guidelines. Minor conflicts were disclosed during GDG meetings without further action. A summary of DOI statements and conflict management is included in the guideline annex. Priority questions and outcomes were aligned with the ANC guideline and informed by a scoping exercise of existing clinical practice guidelines and systematic reviews. Pregnant women’s desire for a positive pregnancy experience, defined as maintaining physical and sociocultural normality, achieving a healthy pregnancy and fetus, transitioning effectively to positive labor and birth, and achieving positive motherhood, guided the overarching principle of the ANC guideline recommendations. Evidence to support the recommendation was derived from a new systematic review on antenatal ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy. Evidence was evaluated using standardized procedures, and evidence profiles were prepared, including GRADE tables assessing the certainty of evidence. A 2021 qualitative systematic review informed the values, equity, acceptability, and feasibility criteria of the evidence-to-decision (EtD) framework. Cost-effectiveness reviews were identified through PubMed searches. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the certainty of quantitative evidence, rating it as high, moderate, low, or very low based on established criteria. Qualitative evidence was appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which evaluates methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The WHO Steering Group supervised the preparation of the evidence summary and profile using the DECIDE framework, which systematically considers research evidence on interventions based on six criteria: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The graded evidence was interpreted according to guidance from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care Group. GDG members reviewed the evidence summary before the online meeting in June 2021. During the meeting, they discussed and made judgments on the impact of interventions for each EtD criterion. These judgments were summarized before finalizing the recommendation and remarks.
